title: Religious practice functions as relational infrastructure for some married couples even as religious participation declines
source_unit: Institute for Family Studies, The Devout Difference: Religion, Marital Quality, and Sex Among Americans, September 25, 2026
geography: United States; married adults ages 20-54, with General Social Survey trend comparisons

observations.period: 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey and General Social Survey comparisons, published September 25, 2026; relational outcomes

denominator.unit: married U.S. adults ages 20-54; comparison groups defined by religious affiliation and attendance; full 2026 survey denominator not stated on the public report summary

churchgoing_catholic_happy.unit: percent of churchgoing Catholics reported as very or extremely happily married

churchgoing_protestant_happy.unit: percent of churchgoing Protestants reported as very or extremely happily married

nonreligious_happy.unit: percent of non-religious husbands and wives reported as very or extremely happily married

marital_permanence_odds.unit: adjusted odds ratio for high marital satisfaction among respondents endorsing marital permanence, controlling for education, race, age, and sex

relational_infrastructure.value: Among the groups studied, religious attendance, shared norms, and repeated communal practice are associated with stronger reported marital quality.

observations.method: IFS report combining the 2026 Religion and Family Survey with General Social Survey trend comparisons; the public summary reports adjusted associations but does not provide the full survey sample size on the page reviewed.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates are observational and may reflect selection, age, marriage entry, education, social support, family composition, shared values, or other differences between churchgoing and secular couples; they do not establish that attendance causes marital happiness.
observations.subgroup: Married U.S. adults ages 20-54, split by Catholic, Protestant, nonreligious, and church-attendance categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with stronger relationships, more stable family circumstances, or compatible values may be more likely to attend religious services; institutional support may be one pathway among several.

observations.period: General Social Survey 1972-2024 trend comparison, published September 25, 2026; religious participation and weekly sex

denominator.unit: General Social Survey respondents in the report’s longitudinal comparison; married respondents ages 20-54 analyzed by attendance

frequent_churchgoing_decline.unit: reported share attending religious services several times a month or more, 1972 to 2024

weekly_sex_churchgoing.unit: percent of regular churchgoing married adults ages 20-54 reporting sex at least weekly in the current comparison

weekly_sex_nonreligious.unit: percent of nonreligious married adults ages 20-54 reporting sex at least weekly in the current comparison

institutional_shrinkage_persistence.value: Religious participation has declined at the population level while stronger relational outcomes remain concentrated among those who continue to participate regularly.

observations.method: Report comparison of General Social Survey historical data with the 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey; the two sources are not treated as one repeated panel.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-period comparisons may reflect changes in wording, age composition, marriage selection, reporting norms, and survey design; weekly sex is self-reported and not a direct measure of relationship wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Married U.S. adults ages 20-54, categorized by religious attendance or affiliation.
observations.counterinterpretation: The observed gap may be driven by selection into marriage, religion, or stable partnerships rather than religious practice itself.

observations.period: 2026 IFS Religion and Family Survey, published September 25, 2026; shared practice and sexual satisfaction

denominator.unit: married U.S. adults ages 20-54; full 2026 survey denominator not stated on the public report summary

churchgoing_weekly_sex.unit: percent of regular churchgoing spouses reporting weekly sex, compared with 48% among secular spouses

churchgoing_sex_satisfaction.value: 45%-55% by religious group among churchgoing spouses, versus 35%-40% among comparison groups
churchgoing_sex_satisfaction.unit: reported share rating sex life excellent or very good

prayer_satisfaction_odds.unit: reported odds ratio for sexual satisfaction among daily-praying Catholic and Protestant respondents versus those not regularly praying

shared_meaning_route.value: The report interprets shared ritual, commitment, and value alignment as possible relational supports, but the design cannot distinguish ritual effects from selection and relationship quality.

observations.method: Cross-sectional IFS Religion and Family Survey with reported subgroup comparisons and adjusted odds ratios.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide all questionnaire, sample, weighting, or model details; sexual frequency and satisfaction are self-reports and associations are not causal effects.
observations.subgroup: Married Catholic and Protestant spouses, nonreligious comparison groups, and respondents categorized by prayer or church attendance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared values, marital commitment, age, partner selection, and social support may jointly explain the observed associations.

related_sources.claim: Official IFS report page containing the 2026 Religion and Family Survey findings, GSS comparisons, subgroup results, and reported adjusted associations.
The General Social Survey is the historical survey source used for selected trend comparisons; the IFS report remains the interpretive source for the presented comparison.

boundary: This record adds a relational-social-infrastructure route: regular religious practice and shared marital norms are associated with higher reported marital quality and sexual satisfaction among the groups studied even as participation declines. It does not establish a causal faith effect, universal religious advantage, or that sexual frequency equals relationship wellbeing. Public report materials do not provide the full 2026 survey sample and model documentation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official IFS report page was reviewed for the report date, survey frame, marital-quality estimates, church-attendance comparisons, GSS trend claims, sexual-satisfaction measures, adjusted associations, and public methodological limits.
